entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen17309" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen17310" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17311" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17311" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17310" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17312" type="x-p"/> Job laments his present condition, and gives an affecting account of his former prosperity, having property in abundance, being surrounded by a numerous family, and enjoying every mark of the approbation of God, <reference osisRef="Job.29.1-Job.29.6">Job 29:1-6</reference>. Speaks of the respect he had from the young, <reference osisRef="Job.29.7">Job 29:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.29.8">Job 29:8</reference>; and from the nobles, <reference osisRef="Job.29.9">Job 29:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.29.10">Job 29:10</reference>. Details his conduct as a magistrate and judge in supporting the poor, and repressing the wicked, <reference osisRef="Job.29.11-Job.29.17">Job 29:11-17</reference>; his confidence, general prosperity, and respect, <reference osisRef="Job.29.18-Job.29.25">Job 29:18-25</reference>.
entries.content_plain: Introduction Job laments his present condition, and gives an affecting account of his former prosperity, having property in abundance, being surrounded by a numerous family, and enjoying every mark of the approbation of God, Job 29:1-6 . entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen17312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17313" type="x-p"/> O that I were as in months past - Job seems here to make an apology for his complaints, by taking a view of his former prosperity, which was very great, but was now entirely at an end. He shows that it was not removed because of any bad use he had made of it; and describes how he behaved himself before God and man, and how much, for justice, benevolence, and mercy, he was esteemed and honored by the wise and good. <div eID="gen17313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17314" type="x-p"/> Preserved me - Kept, guarded, and watched over me.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen17314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17315" type="x-p"/> When his candle shined upon my head - Alluding most probably to the custom of illuminating festival or assembly rooms by lamps pendant from the ceiling. These shone literally on the heads of the guests. <div eID="gen17315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17316" type="x-p"/> By his light I walked through darkness - His light - prosperity and peace - continued to illuminate my way. If adversity came, I had always the light of God to direct me. Almost all the nations of the world have represented their great men as having a nimbus or Divine glory about their heads, which not only signified the honor they had, but was also an emblem of the inspiration of the Almighty.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen17316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17317" type="x-p"/> The days of my youth - The original word rather means in the days of my winter, חרפי charpi, from חרף charaph, "to strip or make bare." Mr. Harmer supposes the rainy season is intended, when the fields, etc., parched up by long drought, are revived by the plentiful showers. Mr. Good thinks the word as found in the Arabic, which means top or summit, and which he translates perfection, is that which should be preferred. Others think the autumnal state is meant, when he was loaded with prosperity, as the trees are with ripe fruit. <div eID="gen17317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17318" type="x-p"/> The secret of God was upon my tabernacle - בסוד אלוה besod Eloah, "the secret assembly of God," meaning probably the same thing that is spoken of in the beginning of this book, the sons of God, the devout people, presenting themselves before God. It is not unlikely that such a secret assembly of God Job had in his own house; where he tells us, in the next verse, "The Almighty was with him, and his children were about him." Mr. Good translates differently: When God fortified my tent over me; supposing that the Hebrew סוד sod is the Arabic sud, "a barrier or fortification." Either will make a good sense.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen17319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17320" type="x-p"/> When I went out to the gate - Courts of justice were held at the gates or entrances of the cities of the East; and Job, being an emir, was supreme magistrate: and here he speaks of his going to the gate to administer justice. <div eID="gen17320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17321" type="x-p"/> I prepared my seat in the street - I administered judgment openly, in the most public manner, and none could say that I, in any case, perverted justice. Mr. Good translates: - "As I went forth the city rejoiced at me, as I took my seat abroad."

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen17321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17322" type="x-p"/> The young men saw me, and hid themselves - From all classes of persons I had the most marked respect. The Young, through modesty and bashfulness, shrunk back, and were afraid to meet the eye of their prince; and the Aged rose from their seats when I entered the place of judgment. These were the elders of the people, who also sat with the judge, and assisted in all legal cases.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen17323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17324" type="x-p"/> The nobles held their peace - Princes שרים sarim, and Nobles, נגידים negidim, must have been two different classes of the great men of Idumea. שר sar, Prince, director, or ruler, was probably the head of a township, or what we would call a magistrate of a particular district. נגיד nagid, a Noble, or one of those who had the privilege of standing before, or in the presence of, the chief ruler. The participle נגד neged is frequently used to signify before, in the presence of, publicly, openly. And on this account, it is most likely that the noun means one of those nobles or counsellors who were always admitted to the royal presence. Mr. Good thinks that renowned speakers or eminent orators are meant: and others have embraced the same opinion. Job here intimates that his judgment was so sound, his decisions so accredited, and his reasoning power so great, that every person paid him the utmost deference.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen17338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17339" type="x-p"/> I laughed on them, they believed it not - Similar to that expression in the Gospel, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.41">Luk 24:41</reference> : And while they believed not for joy, and wondered, he said - . Our version is sufficiently perspicuous, and gives the true sense of the original, only it should be read in the indicative and not in the subjunctive mood: I laughed on them - they believed it not. We have a similar phrase: The news was too good to be true. <div eID="gen17339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17340" type="x-p"/> The light of my countenance - This evidence of my benevolence and regard. A smile is, metaphorically, the light of the countenance. <div eID="gen17340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17341" type="x-p"/> They cast not down - They gave me no occasion to change my sentiments or feelings towards them. I could still smile upon them, and they were then worthy of my approbation. Their change he refers to in the beginning of the next chapter.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen17341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17342" type="x-p"/> I chose out their way, and sat chief - as a king in the army - I cannot see, with some learned men, that our version of the original is wrong. I have not seen it mended, and I am sure I cannot improve it. The whole verse seems to me to point out Job in his civil, military, and domestic life. As supreme magistrate he chose out their way, adjusted their differences, and sat chief, presiding in all their civil assemblies. As captain general he dwelt as a king in the midst of his troops, preserving order and discipline, and seeing that his fellow soldiers were provided with requisites for their warfare, and the necessaries of life. As a man he did not think himself superior to the meanest offices in domestic life, to relieve or support his fellow creatures; he went about comforting the mourners - visiting the sick and afflicted, and ministering to their wants, and seeing that the wounded were properly attended. Noble Job! Look at him, ye nobles of the earth, ye lieutenants of counties, ye generals of armies, and ye lords of provinces. Look at Job! Imitate his active benevolence, and be healthy and happy. Be as guardian angels in your particular districts, blessing all by your example and your bounty. Send your hunting horses to the plough, your game cocks to the dunghill; and at last live like men and Christians.  <chapter eID="Job.29"/> <div eID="gen17342" type="x-p"/>
